title: I. Plans For Mitya’s Escape
paragraphs: Very early, at nine in the morning, five days after the trial, Alyosha went to see Katerina Ivanovna, to discuss a matter that mattered a great deal to both of them, and to deliver a message. She received him and talked with him in the very room where she had once received Grushenka. In the next room, Ivan Fyodorovitch lay unconscious with a high fever. Right after the scene at the trial, Katerina Ivanovna had ordered the sick, unconscious man carried to her house, ignoring the inevitable gossip and the public's general disapproval. One of the two relatives living with her had left for Moscow immediately after the courtroom scene; the other had stayed. But even if both had gone, Katerina Ivanovna would have held to her resolve and gone on nursing the sick man, sitting by him day and night. Varvinsky and Herzenstube were attending him. The famous doctor had returned to Moscow, refusing to venture an opinion on how the illness would likely end. Though the doctors tried to encourage Katerina Ivanovna and Alyosha, it was clear they couldn't yet offer any real hope of recovery.

Alyosha came to see his sick brother twice a day. But this time he had particularly urgent business, and he could already tell how hard it would be to bring up the subject, and yet he was in a great hurry. He had another appointment that morning he couldn't put off, and there was no time to waste.

They had been talking for a quarter of an hour. Katerina Ivanovna was pale, utterly exhausted, and yet at the same time in a state of hysterical agitation. She had a feeling she already knew why Alyosha had come.

“Don't worry about his decision,” she told Alyosha, with confident emphasis. “One way or another, he's bound to come around to it. He has to escape. That unhappy man, that hero of honor and principle — not him, not Dmitri Fyodorovitch, but the man lying on the other side of that door, who has sacrificed himself for his brother” — Katya added, her eyes flashing — “told me the whole escape plan long ago. You know he's already opened negotiations.... I've told you some of it already.... You see, it will probably happen at the third stopping point from here, when the group of prisoners is being marched off to Siberia. Oh, that's a long way off yet. Ivan Fyodorovitch has already visited the superintendent at the third stop. But we still don't know who'll be in charge of the party, and there's no way to find that out so far in advance. Tomorrow, perhaps, I'll show you the whole plan in detail, the one Ivan Fyodorovitch left with me on the eve of the trial, in case it's needed.... That was when — do you remember? — you found us quarreling. He'd just gone downstairs, but when he saw you I made him come back — do you remember? Do you know what we were quarreling about then?”
“No, I don't,” said Alyosha.

“Of course he didn't tell you. It was about that escape plan. He'd told me the main idea three days before, and we started quarreling about it right away, and kept it up for three days. We quarreled because, when he told me that if Dmitri Fyodorovitch were convicted he'd escape abroad with that creature, I flew into a fury on the spot — I can't tell you why, I don't even know myself why.... Oh, of course, I was furious about that creature — furious that she, too, would go abroad with Dmitri!” Katerina Ivanovna exclaimed suddenly, her lips trembling with anger. “The moment Ivan Fyodorovitch saw how furious I was about that woman, he instantly assumed I was jealous of Dmitri, that I still loved him. That's how our first quarrel started. I wouldn't explain myself, I couldn't bring myself to ask forgiveness. I couldn't bear the thought that a man like that could suspect me of still loving that... when I myself had told him, long before, that I didn't love Dmitri, that I loved no one but him! It was purely my resentment at that creature that made me angry with him. Three days later, the evening you came, he brought me a sealed envelope, which I was to open at once if anything happened to him. Oh — he already foresaw his illness! He told me the envelope held the details of the escape, and that if he died, or fell dangerously ill, I was to save Mitya on my own. Then he left me money — nearly ten thousand — the very notes the prosecutor mentioned in his speech, having learned from someone that he'd sent them to be cashed. I was tremendously moved to find that Ivan Fyodorovitch hadn't given up on the idea of saving his brother, and was confiding this escape plan to me, even while he was still jealous of me, still convinced I loved Mitya. Oh, that was a sacrifice! No — you can't understand the greatness of such self-sacrifice, Alexey Fyodorovitch. I wanted to fall at his feet in reverence, but it occurred to me at once that he'd take it for nothing more than my joy at the thought of Mitya being saved — and he certainly would have thought exactly that! — and I was so outraged at the mere possibility of such an unjust thought on his part that I lost my temper all over again, and instead of kissing his feet, flew into a rage instead! Oh, I'm a wretched creature! It's my character, my terrible, wretched character! Oh, you'll see — I'll end up driving him away too, toward some other woman he can get along with better, the way it happened with Dmitri. But... no, I couldn't bear that, I'd kill myself. And when you came in that day, and I called out to you and told him to come back, I was so enraged by the look of contempt and hatred he turned on me that — do you remember? — I cried out to you that it was he, he alone, who'd convinced me his brother Dmitri was a murderer! I said that spiteful thing on purpose, to wound him again. He had never, never convinced me his brother was a murderer. On the contrary — it was I who convinced him! Oh, my vile temper was the cause of everything! I paved the way for that hideous scene at the trial. He wanted to show me he was an honorable man, that even if I loved his brother, he wouldn't destroy him out of revenge or jealousy. So he came to the court.... I'm the cause of it all — I alone am to blame!”

Katya had never made confessions like this to Alyosha before, and he sensed she'd reached that point of unbearable suffering where even the proudest heart is forced to crush its own pride and give way to grief. Oh, Alyosha knew of another terrible source of her present misery, though she'd carefully hidden it from him in the days since the trial — but it would somehow have been too painful for him if she'd sunk so low as to speak to him about it now. She was suffering over her ‘betrayal’ at the trial, and Alyosha sensed her conscience was pushing her to confess it to him — to him, Alyosha — with tears, with cries, writhing on the floor in hysterics. But he dreaded that moment and wanted, above all, to spare her. It made the errand he'd come on all the harder. He turned the conversation back to Mitya.

“It's all right, it's all right, don't worry about him!” she began again, sharply, stubbornly. “All that is only temporary — I know him, I know his heart better than anyone. You can be sure he'll agree to escape. It won't happen right away — he'll have time to make up his mind to it. By then Ivan Fyodorovitch will be well and will manage the whole thing himself, so I won't have to do anything with it. Don't worry — he'll agree to run. He's already agreed, in fact — do you suppose he'd give up that creature? And they won't let her go to him there, so he's bound to escape. It's you he's most afraid of — he's afraid you won't approve of his escaping, on moral grounds. But you must be generous enough to allow it, if your blessing matters so much to him,” Katya added, with a touch of spite. She paused, and smiled.

“He talks about some hymn,” she went on, “some cross he has to bear, some duty — I remember Ivan Fyodorovitch told me a great deal about it, and if you only knew how he talked!” Katya cried suddenly, unable to hold back her feeling. “If you knew how he loved that wretched man, right there while he was telling me — and how he hated him too, in that same moment, perhaps! And I listened to his story, to his tears, with sneering contempt. Brute — yes, I'm a brute. I'm the cause of his fever. But that man in prison isn't even capable of suffering,” Katya concluded irritably. “Can a man like that really suffer? Men like him never suffer!”

There was a note of hatred and contemptuous revulsion in her words. And yet it was she who had betrayed him. ‘Maybe it's because she senses how she's wronged him that she hates him, at moments like this,’ Alyosha thought to himself. He hoped it really was only ‘at moments.’ He caught a challenging note in Katya's last words, but he didn't rise to it.

“I sent for you this morning to get your promise that you'll persuade him yourself. Or do you also think escaping would be dishonorable, cowardly, or something... unchristian, perhaps?” Katya added, even more defiantly.

“Oh, no. I'll tell him everything,” Alyosha muttered. “He's asking you to come and see him today,” he blurted out suddenly, looking her straight in the face. She started, and drew back a little from him on the sofa.
“Me? Is that really possible?” she faltered, going pale.

“It's possible, and it ought to happen!” Alyosha began, growing more animated, speaking with emphasis. “He needs you especially right now. I wouldn't have raised the subject and troubled you if it weren't necessary. He's ill, he's beside himself, he keeps asking for you. He doesn't want to be reconciled with you — he only wants you to come and show yourself in his doorway. So much has happened to him since that day. He understands now that he's wronged you beyond all measure. He isn't asking your forgiveness — ‘It's impossible to forgive me,’ he says himself — only that you show yourself in his doorway.”
“It's all so sudden....” Katya faltered. “I've had a feeling, these past few days, that you'd come with exactly this message. I knew he'd ask me to come. It's impossible!”

“Let it be impossible — do it anyway. Just think: he's realized, for the first time in his life, how deeply he's wounded you; he never fully understood it before. He said, ‘If she refuses to come, I'll be unhappy my whole life.’ Do you hear that? Even though he's been sentenced to twenty years of hard labor, he's still making plans to be happy — isn't that pitiful? Think — you must visit him. Even though he's ruined, he's innocent,” broke from Alyosha like a challenge. “His hands are clean — there's no blood on them! For the sake of everything he's still going to suffer, visit him now. Go — send him off on his way into the darkness. Stand in his doorway, that's all.... You ought to do it, you ought to!” Alyosha finished, leaning hard on the word ‘ought.’
“I ought to... but I can't....” Katya moaned. “He'll look at me.... I can't.”
“Your eyes ought to meet. How will you go on living your whole life, if you don't make up your mind to do this now?”
“Better to suffer my whole life.”
“You ought to go, you ought to go,” Alyosha repeated, with merciless insistence.
“But why today, why right now?... I can't leave our patient—”
“You can spare a moment. It will only take a moment. If you don't come, he'll be delirious by tonight. I wouldn't lie to you — have pity on him!”
“Have pity on me!” Katya said, with bitter reproach, and burst into tears.
“Then you'll come,” Alyosha said firmly, seeing her tears. “I'll go and tell him you're coming right away.”
“No — don't you dare tell him that,” Katya cried in alarm. “I'll come, but don't tell him beforehand, because I might go there and not go in.... I don't know yet—”
Her voice gave out. She gasped for breath. Alyosha got up to leave.
“And what if I run into someone?” she said suddenly, in a low voice, going white again.
“That's exactly why you should go now — to avoid running into anyone. There'll be no one there, I can promise you that. We'll be expecting you,” he finished firmly, and left the room.
